head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: The lowest bit of an even number is 0
Sets every bit that is set in x; bits never get cleared
`0 | x = x`, and it is also the answer when there are no even numbers

blocks.h: Why does OR need no special case?
p: OR is associative and commutative with identity 0, so folding the even numbers in any order gives their combined OR, and an empty selection naturally leaves 0, which is the required output.

3688.takeaway: OR-accumulate only the even numbers; the empty result is 0 automatically.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Keep going while the multiple is present
Stops at the first multiple that is missing

blocks.h: Why does the loop end quickly?
p: `nums` has at most n elements, so among the first n+1 multiples of k at least one is missing; the loop runs at most n+1 times. A set makes each check O(1), whereas scanning the list would give O(n²).

3718.takeaway: Walk through k, 2k, 3k, … and stop at the first one not in the set of numbers.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: The common target: raising is the only allowed move, so nothing can go below the maximum
Sum if all elements were equal to the maximum

blocks.h: Why is the maximum the best target?
p: Each move adds 1 to a single element, so the final common value must be at least the maximum. Each element needs `target − x` moves, so the total is `n·target − sum`, which grows with the target: the smallest total comes from the smallest possible target, the maximum.

3736.takeaway: Only increases are allowed, so raise everything to the maximum: moves = max × n − sum.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: All ordered selections of 4 DIFFERENT words (from `itertools`)
The four roles (top, left, right, bottom) need distinct words
Letter at each corner is shared by two words
Sort the list of lists lexicographically
Lists compare element by element: top first, then left, right, bottom

p: `['able', 'area', 'echo', 'also']` → [['able', 'area', 'echo', 'also'], ['area', 'able', 'also', 'echo']]:

With n ≤ 15 words there are at most 15·14·13·12 = 32,760 ordered selections, each checked in O(1). Because `permutations` generates ordered tuples, every assignment of words to roles is tried exactly once, and the conditions pick out the valid squares.

bullets: Space: O(1) extra besides the output.

3799.takeaway: Try every ordered choice of four distinct words and test the four corner letters; sort the valid squares.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Distances from s to all nodes
BFS (Breadth-First Search) on an unweighted tree
The three distances in increasing order
Puts the largest in `c`, the hypotenuse candidate
No square roots, no float rounding

p: Star: centre 0 with leaves 1, 2, 3; targets 1, 2, 3 → 3 special nodes:

Every node needs its distance to each of the three targets. In a tree, one BFS from each target gives all distances in O(n), so the total is 3 BFS passes plus an O(n) scan, rather than computing pairwise distances per node.

3820.takeaway: BFS (Breadth-First Search) from each of the three targets, then test a² + b² = c² on the sorted distances of each node.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: FIFO (First In, First Out): the earliest is matched first; `popleft` is O(1)
Lazy deletion: don't search the deque
Drop cancelled riders when they reach the front

p: Calls in order:

Removing an arbitrary rider from the middle of a deque costs O(n). Recording the cancellation in a set is O(1), and a cancelled rider is discarded only when it reaches the front during a match. Each rider is popped at most once, so matching is O(1) amortised.

3829.takeaway: Two FIFO queues for riders and drivers, with cancelled riders recorded in a set and skipped when they reach the front.

Number of choice sequences giving each current value
The three actions: leave, multiply, divide
Each state spawns up to three states
Ways to end at exactly k

p: `[2,3,2]`, `k = 6` → 2 (the sequences multiply, multiply, leave and leave, multiply, multiply both reach 6). Reachable values and their counts after each number:

blocks.h: Why Fraction and a dictionary of values?
p: Many different choice sequences lead to the same value, so merging them by value keeps the number of states small (far fewer than 3ⁿ). `Fraction` keeps division exact (1/2 stays 1/2), and two different paths reaching 1/2 are recognised as equal; floats could differ by rounding.

bullets: Time: O(3ⁿ) worst case, much less in practice because equal values merge.

3850.takeaway: DP over the set of reachable exact values (Fractions) with counts: each number multiplies, divides or leaves the value.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Sum of the elements before index i
Product of the elements after index i
The left sum never exceeds `sum(nums)`, so any product above it can never match
Keeps numbers small and avoids huge integers (and still compares correctly)
First match from the left is the smallest index

p: `[2,1,2]` → 1 (suffix products with cap 6: `[4, 2, 2, 1]`):

Products of up to 10⁵ numbers explode. But the left sum is at most `sum(nums)`, so once a suffix product exceeds `sum(nums) + 1` it can never equal any prefix sum. Capping at `cap` keeps every product small without changing any comparison, and later products of capped values stay at least `cap`. The result agrees with a direct product computation on 500 random arrays: True.

3862.takeaway: Prefix sum against suffix products, with products capped at sum(nums) + 1 so they stay small.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Counts of each value in each list
Free swaps within a list mean only counts matter
Total count of v is odd
Both final lists must contain v the same number of times, so the total must be even
Copies of v that must move from list 1 to list 2
Each list must end with half of the total
The surplus in list 2 is moved by the same swaps in the other direction
All values that appear in either list

blocks.h: Why do the counts decide the cost?
p: Swapping within a list is free, so the lists can be arranged freely; the only paid operation exchanges nums1[i] with nums2[i] at cost 1. The final lists must be equal, so each value must appear equally often in both lists, which requires an even total. Each paid swap moves one surplus copy of a value from list 1 to list 2 while moving one surplus copy of another value back, so the cost is the total number of surplus copies in list 1 (counting each value's excess over its target half). Summing `(c1 − c2) // 2` over values with c1 > c2 gives exactly that. A breadth-first search over all swaps agrees with this formula on 300 random small inputs.

3868.takeaway: Both lists must hold each value equally often; the cost is the total surplus copies that must move from list 1 to list 2.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Indexes of the most recent 1 and most recent 2
Only the nearest earlier partner matters for each new element
Distance from this 1 back to the last 2
Distance from this 2 back to the last 1

blocks.h: Why only the most recent partner?
p: For a new 1 at index i, the nearest 2 to its left is the latest 2 seen; any earlier 2 is farther away. Pairs where the 2 comes after the 1 are handled when the 2 is reached (with the latest 1). So every closest pair is examined once in a single left-to-right pass.

3880.takeaway: Track the last index of 1 and of 2; each new element pairs with the nearest earlier partner of the other value.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Gaps to the left and right neighbours
Strictly increasing, so gaps are positive; missing neighbour = infinity
The closest neighbour is on the right (the left wins ties)
Cheapest cost to walk from 0 to i+1 moving right
Step i → i+1 costs 1 if i+1 is i's closest neighbour, otherwise the gap `gr` (jump cost)
`left[i - 1] = left[i] + (1 if not closest_right else gl)`
Cheapest cost to walk from n−1 to i−1 moving left

blocks.h: Why prefix sums in each direction?
p: Moving from l to r (l < r) is best done by walking one index at a time: the cheapest way to cover each step is independent of the others, so the total is the sum of per-step costs, stored as prefix sums. The step i → i+1 costs 1 when i+1 is the closest neighbour of i and the gap otherwise; the leftward steps are mirrored. A direct Dijkstra search over all jumps agrees with the formula on 200 random cases: True.

3919.takeaway: Per-step costs along the line (1 for a closest-neighbour step, the gap otherwise) stored as prefix sums in each direction.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: DP (Dynamic Programming) over the last day
Buy on day i, sell on day j
Best profit that ends early enough to buy again on day i
After selling on day s, the next buy is allowed from day s + cooldown + 1, so the previous sale must be on day ≤ i − cooldown − 1
Profit of this trade including the holding cost for j − i days
The cost depends on how long the share is held

p: prices `[1,5,3]`, `cooldown = 1`, `costs = [0,1,2]` → 3:

head: Day j
best[j]
Reason
rows: buy day 0, sell day 2: 3 − 1 − 2 = 0; or keep best[1]

blocks.h: Why best[i − cooldown − 1] and an O(n²) loop?
p: Selling on day j after buying on day i, with the previous sale on day s, requires s + cooldown + 1 ≤ i, i.e. s ≤ i − cooldown − 1. So the best total for the prefix before the buy is `best[i − cooldown − 1]`, and the trade adds its own profit. The holding cost depends on j − i, so no simple monotone trick applies and all (i, j) pairs are tried: O(n²) for n ≤ 1000.

4069.takeaway: DP over prefixes: best[j] = max(best[j−1], best[i − cooldown − 1] + profit of buying on day i and selling on day j).
